sources.entry: URL shortening is the action of shortening a URL to make it substantially shorter and still direct to the required page. Before hosting one, please see disadvantages of URL shorteners.

summary.name: URL shortening (Wikipedia)
summary.one_liner: A Wikipedia article explaining URL shortening: how redirect-based short links work, their uses, history, and abuse, privacy, and linkrot risks.
use_cases: Understanding how short links redirect to long URLs
Deciding whether to host a private URL shortener
Checking risks before clicking a shortened link
Shortening links for SMS or character-limited messages
Researching history of URL shortening services
summary.what_it_does: The article describes URL shortening as a technique where a long URL is replaced by a shorter one that redirects via HTTP status codes (301, 302, 307, 308) to the original page. It covers key generation methods such as base 36 and base 62, custom keys, and which URI schemes can be shortened. It also reviews history from TinyURL (2002) through Google's goo.gl shutdown, plus abuse, blocklisting, privacy exposure of shortened links, and linkrot. It is a reference article, not a product, and includes a note on the awesome-selfhosted listing that points to disadvantages before hosting one.
notable: Covers redirect status codes and base-36/base-62 key generation
Documents the goo.gl shutdown timeline and linkrot risks
Lists notable services such as bit.ly, TinyURL, t.co, and w.wiki
Discusses privacy risks such as brute-force discovery of short links
caveats: Shortened links can expire or break if the service stops working (linkrot)
Short links can hide malicious destinations and are often blocked by spam filters and sites
